samples.text:
Traffic congestion is a serious problem in most big cities around the world. Some people believe that if public transport is completely free, more people will use it and the traffic will decrease. I agree with this idea for the most part.

The first reason is that money is important for many people when they choose how to travel. If a person have to pay for the bus every day, it can be expensive, especially for students and workers with low salary. So they prefer to use motorbike or car. But if buses and trains are free, many of them will leave their cars at home. This will make the roads less crowded and also reduce the air pollution, which is a big problem in cities like mine.

Another reason is that free transport is fair for everyone. Poor people can travel to their job, to hospital or to school without worrying about the cost. This can help them to find better jobs and improve their life. In addition, the city will save time because there is no need to sell tickets and check them.

However, there are some problems with this idea. The government need a lot of money to run the buses and trains, so it may have to increase the taxes. Also, if the service is not good, people will still use their cars even it is free. For example, if the bus is always late or very crowded, people don't want to use it.

In conclusion, I agree that making public transport free can reduce traffic congestion, because it encourages people to stop using private cars. However, the government must also improve the quality of the service, otherwise the plan will not be successful.
samples.why: Clear position with relevant reasons · some ideas are general and not fully extended · linking is mechanical but effective · adequate vocabulary with some repetition · several grammar errors that do not reduce clarity.

samples.text:
Many cities suffer from severe traffic congestion, and one proposed solution is to make public transport entirely free for passengers. Although this policy has some clear attractions, I largely disagree that it is the best way to tackle congestion, because cost is rarely the main factor that keeps drivers off buses and trains.

Supporters of free travel argue that removing fares would encourage people to switch from private cars. This may be true for some groups, such as students and low-income workers, for whom daily fares represent a significant expense. Free services would also make cities more inclusive, since everyone could reach jobs, schools and hospitals regardless of their income.

However, most car owners choose to drive because it is faster, more comfortable or more convenient, not because public transport is too expensive. If buses are overcrowded, unreliable or do not reach the suburbs where people live, abolishing fares will change very little. In fact, some cities that have introduced free transport found that many new passengers were people who previously walked or cycled, which does nothing to reduce the number of cars on the road.

Furthermore, fares provide an important source of funding. Without this income, transport authorities would depend entirely from taxation, and in times of budget pressure they might be forced to cut routes or delay improvements. This could make the service less attractive and eventually encourage more people to drive.

A more effective approach would be to invest in frequent, reliable services and combine this with measures that make driving less appealing, such as congestion charges or limited parking in city centres. Reduced fares for certain groups could also be offered.

In conclusion, while free public transport would benefit some residents, I do not believe it would significantly reduce congestion on its own. Improving service quality and discouraging car use are likely to be far more effective.
samples.why: Clear, consistent position · main ideas developed with relevant support, though one example is generalised · well-organised paragraphs · appropriate range of cohesive devices · some less common vocabulary · mostly accurate grammar.

samples.text:
Abolishing fares on buses, trams and trains is sometimes presented as a simple remedy for urban traffic congestion. While I accept that free public transport has genuine social merits, I disagree that it is, by itself, an effective way of reducing congestion, and I believe the money it would require could be spent more productively.

The appeal of fare-free travel is easy to understand. It removes a cost that weighs most heavily on low-income households, simplifies journeys for occasional users and sends a strong public signal that the city values collective transport over private cars. For young people and those on modest wages, eliminating fares might well be the deciding factor that makes the bus a realistic alternative.

The difficulty is that motorists are generally less sensitive to price than to time and convenience. A commuter who drives does so because the car offers a direct, predictable journey; if the equivalent trip by public transport involves two changes and a long wait, making it free will rarely alter that calculation. Experience in several cities suggests that fare-free schemes tend to attract people who would otherwise have walked or cycled, which increases demand on the network without taking many cars off the road.

There is also the question of funding. Ticket revenue typically covers a substantial part of operating costs, and replacing it would place a permanent burden on public budgets. When finances tighten, it is service frequency and maintenance that usually suffer first, precisely the qualities that persuade drivers to switch.

Congestion is therefore better addressed through a combination of measures: sustained investment in faster, more frequent services, dedicated bus lanes, and policies such as road pricing that reflect the true cost of driving. Targeted discounts can protect those on the lowest incomes without sacrificing essential revenue.

In conclusion, free public transport may be socially desirable, but as a strategy for reducing congestion it promises more than it is likely to deliver.
samples.why: Well-developed, nuanced argument with a clear position · ideas logically sequenced and fully supported · skilful paragraphing and cohesion · precise, natural vocabulary · wide range of accurate complex structures.
